exhibits.title: The Direction-Glass
exhibits.text:
Hold any weight-change up to this glass and it does not show you the numbers — it shows you the DIRECTIONS. Where a matrix has been rich and varied, many spokes blaze; where its work is truly simple, only a few spokes shine and the rest dim to nothing. Magister Quillon set it here for a single reason: to make visible the fact on which this whole floor rests. An update matrix — the change we would make to a frozen weight — is almost never a full, dense turning of every direction. Its energy pools into a HANDFUL of dominant directions, and the long tail of the rest is nearly zero.

The mathematics behind the glass is the Singular Value Decomposition. Any matrix, of any shape, factors as delta-W = U * Sigma * V^T. The columns of U and V are orthonormal directions — an input direction paired with an output direction — and Sigma is a diagonal of non-negative singular values sigma_1 >= sigma_2 >= ... >= 0, each measuring HOW MUCH the matrix stretches along its paired direction. A large sigma is a direction that matters; a sigma near zero is a direction the matrix barely touches. The glass simply lights each spoke in proportion to its sigma.

The reason this floor exists: for a fine-tuning update, the singular values DECAY FAST. A few are large, then a steep cliff, then a long tail hugging zero. That is the whole justification for low rank — study the plinths to see why keeping only the bright spokes is not a crude shortcut but the provably best approximation you can make, and why LoRA reaches the same place WITHOUT ever building this decomposition.

exhibits.title: What the SVD Says
exhibits.text:
Every matrix has a Singular Value Decomposition. For an update delta-W of shape (d, k):

  delta-W = U * Sigma * V^T

U is (d, d) and V is (k, k), both orthonormal (their columns are perpendicular unit directions); Sigma is (d, k), zero everywhere but its diagonal, which holds the singular values sigma_1 >= sigma_2 >= ... >= 0. Each sigma_i is the GAIN of the matrix along the i-th direction: how far it stretches an input aligned with column i of V, sending it toward column i of U.

The key empirical fact for fine-tuning UPDATES: these singular values decay fast. A few dominant sigmas carry almost all of the update's energy; the rest fall away toward zero. So keep only the top r directions — set the tail to zero:

  delta-W ~= U_r * Sigma_r * V_r^T

where U_r is the first r columns of U, Sigma_r the top r singular values, V_r the first r columns of V. The Eckart-Young theorem guarantees this truncation is the BEST possible rank-r approximation of delta-W in the least-squares sense — no other rank-r matrix is closer.

Now group the factors: let B = U_r * Sigma_r (shape d x r) and A = V_r^T (shape r x k). Then delta-W ~= B * A. This is EXACTLY the shape of a LoRA adapter. Two thin matrices, one tall and one wide, meeting at a narrow waist of width r. The theory of SVD tells you the low-rank form is not merely possible — for an update whose singular values decay, it is nearly lossless.

exhibits.title: Learned, Not Computed
exhibits.text:
Here is the refinement the careless student misses. The SVD on the pedestal beside you explains WHY a rank-r update suffices — but LoRA does not perform it. LoRA never forms delta-W at all. It never computes a decomposition, never truncates a Sigma, never so much as looks at the full update matrix.

Instead it ASSUMES the useful update is approximately low-rank, PARAMETERIZES it directly as a product B * A of two thin matrices of chosen rank r, initializes them (B at zero, A random), and LEARNS their entries by gradient descent — minimising the TASK LOSS, exactly as any weight is trained. The frozen base weight W sits untouched; only B and A receive gradients.

So the two roads differ in their OBJECTIVE, though they arrive near the same country:

  - SVD truncation is given a target matrix delta-W and finds the rank-r matrix CLOSEST to it (a reconstruction objective).
  - LoRA is given a task and finds the rank-r matrix that best REDUCES the loss (a task objective). There is no delta-W handed to it to reconstruct; the good update is discovered, not approximated.

SVD is the THEORY — the reason a few directions are enough — not a step in the pipeline. Remember the one-line creed of this hall: LoRA assumes the useful update is roughly low-rank, parameterizes it as rank-r, and learns it directly.

exhibits.title: Two Roads to a Rank-r Update
exhibits.spec:
graph TD
  DW["full update delta-W"] --> SVD["take SVD: U Sigma V^T"]
  SVD --> TR["keep top r: Eckart-Young"]
  TR --> RU["rank-r update B*A"]
  TASK["task + loss"] --> LRN["learn thin B, A by gradient descent"]
  LRN --> RU
  RU --> OUT["W + B*A"]
exhibits.caption: Left road (theory): given a full update delta-W, take its SVD and truncate to the top r singular directions; Eckart-Young makes this the best rank-r approximation. Right road (LoRA in practice): never form delta-W at all — directly learn thin B and A from the task loss by gradient descent. Different objectives — reconstruct a given matrix vs. minimise a loss — converging on the same rank-r shape B*A. LoRA walks only the right road; the left road merely explains why the right one works.

exhibits.title: The Spectrum Read
exhibits.caption: Hold an update to the Direction-Glass and this is what its spokes would read. LEFT: the singular values of a fine-tuning delta-W, sorted largest to smallest. A few blaze — 8.2, 5.1, 3.7 — then the curve drops off a cliff at the elbow and the tail hugs zero. The gold line is cumulative energy: by the third direction it has already gathered 93% of everything the update carries. That is the whole license for low rank — the meaningful change lives in a handful of directions, so a rank-r truncation keeps almost all of delta-W and discards near-nothing. RIGHT: the two roads set side by side. The SVD road (theory) is HANDED a full delta-W, factors it exactly as U-Sigma-V-transpose, and keeps the top r — Eckart-Young makes that the closest rank-r matrix, a reconstruction objective. The LoRA road (practice) is handed only a task and its loss; it never forms delta-W at all, but parameterizes thin B and A and learns them by gradient descent — a task objective. Two different aims, one shared low-rank shape B*A at the narrow waist of width r. LoRA walks only the right road; the left merely explains why the right one arrives somewhere good. The values are representative — the SHAPE is the lesson.

exhibits.title: The Elbow — Effective Rank
exhibits.text:
Look again at the spokes of the Direction-Glass and plot their brightness in order: sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3, .... The curve falls, and somewhere it BENDS — a sharp elbow after which the singular values are all but zero. The number of directions BEFORE that elbow is the update's EFFECTIVE RANK: how many directions actually carry the change.

This is the quantity that sets how large r must be. The rule is simple and geometric:

  - FAST decay (a steep cliff after two or three sigmas) means the update lives in a tiny subspace — a tiny r captures nearly all of it. This is the common case for adapting a model to a narrow new task.
  - SLOW decay (a long, gentle slope, many middling sigmas) means the change is spread broadly across directions — no small r captures it well, and r must grow. This happens when the adaptation is a large domain shift, closer to genuine re-learning.

Effective rank is not a formula you evaluate before training; it is the SHAPE of the singular-value spectrum that the useful update WOULD have. It explains, in the next chamber, why r is chosen by sweeping and watching validation: you are hunting for the smallest r that clears the elbow. Fast-decaying spectrum, small dial; broad, flat spectrum, larger dial.
